facts: Eight persons were tried for offences under ss. 148, 307 and 364 both read with ss. 149 and 34 of the Indian Penal Code, by the Additional Sessions Judge, Ferozepur.

The learned Sessions Judge acquitted four of the accused, namely, Het Ram, Teja Ram, Manphul and Surja Ram as he did not think that their presence at the occurrence had been proved beyond reasonable doubt.
He convicted the remaining four, namely, Narain, Jot Ram, Gheru and Jalu under ss. 307 and 364 read with s. 34.
The prosecution case is that one Sultan was the proprietor of a field described in the proceedings as plot No. 97.
Sahi Ram had been a tenant of the land.
On June 14, 1953, Mani Ram a son of the proprietor, arrived at the field on a tractor accompanied by a Tabourer, Moola Ram, with the object of Ploughing it and found Sahi Ram actually ploughing.
Mani Ram turned Sahi Ram out of the field.
Sahi Ram raised a protest but eventually left abandoning his plough on the field.

The defence was that the prosecution case was wholly false and the real facts were as follows: On the date of the occurrence Sahi Ram was ploughing the field when Mani Ram and Raghbir came there and tried to stop him.
There were thus two conflicting versions of the same incident and there were two cross cases based on these separate versions.
issues: Whether the trial had been vitiated by the decision of the Sessions Judge that Raghbir was entitled to refuse to give evidence under Art. 20 of the Constitution.
Whether the failure of the Court to examine Raghbir did not in any way affect the ultimate decision of the case.
petitioner_arguments: The learned Advocate for the appellants confined himself in this Court to a question of law which we now proceed to discuss.
It has to be remembered that we are concerned only with the case in which the appellants had been tried for offences against Mani Ram.
The prosecution did not offer Raghbir as a witness and dropped him.
respondent_arguments: The High Court observed as follows: 'We may assume that Raghbir would not have supported the prosecution story or that he would have admitted to having shot Sahi Ram.'
The fact that he was unwilling to make a statement does not constitute an irregularity in the trial.
Had he been compelled to say something, he would, in all probability, not have told the truth, and the question is how the case would have been affected by his statement?
court_reasoning: The expression of the opinion of the High Court on this matter has not been happily worded.
It seems to us that s. 167 does not help the appellants.
Therefore it seems to us that this is not a case in which evidence can be said to have been rejected within s. 167 of the Evidence Act.
holding: The prosecution did not offer Raghbir as a witness and dropped him.
It is clear from the record that the prosecution, though it had cited Raghbir as a witness, was not very keen to examine him
Therefore it seems to us that this is not a case in which evidence can be said to have been rejected within s. 167 of the Evidence Act.
